sources: Horowitz 2009, Behavioural Processes, "Disambiguating the 'guilty look': salient prompts to a familiar dog behaviour" (abstract): 14 dogs were videotaped; owners gave a command not to eat a treat and left the room; "The results revealed no difference in behaviours associated with the guilty look"; "more such behaviours were seen in trials when owners scolded their dogs"; "The effect of scolding was more pronounced when the dogs were obedient, not disobedient"; the look "is a response to owner cues, rather than that it shows an appreciation of a misdeed"; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19520245/

Ostojic, Tkalcic & Clayton 2015, Behavioural Processes, "Are owners' reports of their dogs' 'guilty look' influenced by the dogs' action and evidence of the misdeed?": 96 owners and dogs; "owners stated that their dog had eaten the food no more than expected by chance"; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4310318/
title: 14 Dogs Tested: Your Dog's Guilty Look May Not Be a Confession 🐶 (Things Living In Your House #65)
description:
Why do dogs look guilty? In a 2009 test of 14 dogs, owners told the dog not to eat a treat and left the room. The "guilty look" was no different whether or not the dog had eaten it. It showed up more when owners scolded, and the effect of scolding was stronger in dogs that had obeyed. In a 2015 study of 96 dogs, owners did no better than chance at telling from the greeting whether their dog had eaten the food. These studies test the look, not what dogs feel.

Sources: Horowitz 2009, Behavioural Processes; Ostojic, Tkalcic & Clayton 2015, Behavioural Processes.
